sheet.howExamined: M8, Paper 1 (no calculator) or Paper 2 (calculator), 50 marks in 75 minutes each; a probability question in almost every series from 2019 to 2026, usually in the second half. Four shapes recur. Two items taken without replacement, 4 marks for the same colour or one of each as one part: a mark for each product, one for adding and one for the answer (Summer 2024 M8 Paper 1 Q11, Summer 2025 M8 Paper 2 Q13, November 2025 M8 Paper 1 Q14). Three colours: 3 marks for both of one colour, then 4 or 5 for different colours, most quickly 1 minus the same colour (November 2022 M8 Paper 2 Q13, November 2023 M8 Paper 1 Q12, Summer 2026 M8 Paper 1 Q12). A tree drawn or completed from sentences in which the second chance depends on the first, a mark for each pair of branches, then 2 for a probability read from it (Summer 2024 M8 Paper 2 Q8, November 2025 M8 Paper 2 Q9, Summer 2026 M8 Paper 2 Q9). Group sizes with a probability for each, 4 marks, answered by counting first (Summer 2024 M8 Paper 2 Q7, November 2024 M8 Paper 2 Q1, November 2025 M8 Paper 1 Q3). The A* end puts a letter in the bag and asks for the equation (Summer 2021 M8 Paper 2 Q11, Summer 2022 M8 Paper 1 Q15). Most bag questions say only 'taken at random'; the second pick is still out of one fewer.
traps: Keeping the first-pick denominator on the second pick, so the item is in effect put back; on Summer 2025 M8 Paper 2 Q13, an A* same-colour question, over 70 per cent had full marks

Lowering the denominator but not the numerator when the same type was taken; Summer 2024 M8 Paper 1 Q11, a non-replacement question the report called difficult, was answered impressively, a majority with full marks
Adding along a branch instead of multiplying (Summer 2024 M8 Paper 1 Q9)
Counting one order of a two-colour outcome instead of both (Summer 2024 M8 Paper 2 Q4; November 2024 M8 Paper 2 Q14)
Multiplying the two branch results instead of adding them
Answering at least one with the probability of none, or with the probability of exactly one
Doing two trials when the question asks for three (Summer 2024 M8 Paper 1 Q9)
Arithmetic slips multiplying simple fractions by hand (Summer 2023 M8 Paper 1 Q11; November 2025 M8 Paper 1 Q14)
Leaving labels off the branches, or writing counts where probabilities go (November 2025 M8 Paper 2 Q6; November 2024 M8 Paper 1 Q7; Summer 2024 M8 Paper 2 Q8)
Using one branch, or three, where the description fits two (Summer 2023 M8 Paper 2 Q9)

Dividing by the whole group when the question chooses from part of it: count the ones who fit, then put that count on the bottom (Summer 2024 M8 Paper 2 Q7; November 2024 M8 Paper 2 Q1; November 2025 M8 Paper 1 Q3, where fewer than half had full marks)
Reading 'two are taken at random' as with replacement: unless the item is put back, the second pick is out of one fewer
Writing a probability as a ratio, or leaving an answer greater than 1 unchecked

(b) Work out the probability that one counter is red and the other is green.

Give each answer as a fraction in its simplest form.

steps.decision: There are $9$ counters, so every first-pick denominator is $9$. Writing both branches down, even the one you may not need, keeps the tree honest.

steps.working: Second pick, after a red: $5 - 1 = 4$ reds are left out of $9 - 1 = 8$ counters, so $P(\text{red}) = \tfrac{4}{8}$ and $P(\text{green}) = \tfrac{4}{8}$.
steps.decision: Without replacement, the counter taken does not come back. The denominator always falls by one; the numerator falls only when the same colour was taken.

options: Because one red has gone, so both the reds and the total are one smaller
Because the total is smaller but the number of reds is unchanged
Because the probabilities stay the same on every pick
whyMenu.explain: A red was removed, so the reds fall from $5$ to $4$ and the total falls from $9$ to $8$. Had a green been taken first, the reds would still be $5$ and only the total would fall.

steps.decision: Along a branch you multiply, because both things have to happen. Cancelling before multiplying keeps the numbers small, which matters on the non-calculator paper.

steps.working: One of each happens two ways: red then green, $\tfrac{5}{9} \times \tfrac{4}{8} = \tfrac{20}{72}$, and green then red, $\tfrac{4}{9} \times \tfrac{5}{8} = \tfrac{20}{72}$.
steps.decision: The question does not say which colour comes first, so both orders count. Missing the second order is the error that turns a full-mark answer into a half one.
Across branches you add, because either one will do. The denominators already match, so only the numerators are added.

steps.working: "At least one star" covers star-then-plain, plain-then-star and star-then-star: three of the four branches.
steps.decision: Three branches to add, or one branch to subtract from 1. The second is quicker and gives fewer chances to slip, so that is the route to take.

options: Because the only outcome without a star is plain then plain
Because the two events are independent
Because at least one means exactly one
whyMenu.explain: Everything that is not 'no stars at all' has at least one star, so the two probabilities add to 1. 'At least one' is never the same as 'exactly one'.

steps.decision: The first plain card leaves $4$ plain out of $7$. This is the single branch that has to be right.
Subtract from 1, not from anything else. As a check, adding the other three branches gives $6/56 + 15/56 + 15/56 = 36/56$, which is the same fraction.

options.text: The two branch probabilities were added instead of multiplied
options.feedback: Adding gives $\tfrac{7}{12} + \tfrac{6}{11} = \tfrac{149}{132}$, which is larger than 1 and so cannot be a probability. Along a branch, multiply.

options.text: The second denominator should have stayed the same
options.feedback: The denominator falling by one is correct without replacement. The problem is the operation, not the denominator.

options.text: Nothing: that is the right answer
options.feedback: A probability can never be greater than 1, and this answer is. That check alone finds the slip.

options.feedback: Two branches end with the school closed: snow then closed, and no snow then closed. Multiply along each and add.

The no-snow branch carries 1 − 0.3 = 0.7, not 0.3.
The two branches are two different ways to reach a closure, so their results are added, not multiplied.

options.feedback: The same colour is 28/90; every other pair is different, so 1 − 28/90 = 31/45.
That is the probability of the same colour. Different colours is what is left when it is taken from 1.
Each mixed pair can come in either order; counting one order of each halves the answer.
That keeps 10 under the second pick, as if the first counter went back.

That is the share of members who are men; it ignores who swims.

parts.stem:
Two sweets are taken at random, without replacement, from the tin of $8$ mints and $5$ toffees.

Work out the probability that one is a mint and the other is a toffee.

Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form.
hints: There are two ways for this to happen.
Work out each order, then add them.
parts.workedSolution: Mint then toffee is $\tfrac{8}{13} \times \tfrac{5}{12} = \tfrac{40}{156}$, and toffee then mint is $\tfrac{5}{13} \times \tfrac{8}{12} = \tfrac{40}{156}$. Adding: $\tfrac{40}{156} + \tfrac{40}{156} = \tfrac{80}{156}$, which is $\tfrac{20}{39}$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is mint first, toffee second. Toffee first then mint is a second way for the same thing to happen, and it has to be added on.
Both denominators stayed at $13$, so the sweet went back in. The second denominator is $12$.

parts.stem:
Two sweets are taken at random, without replacement, from the tin of $8$ mints and $5$ toffees.

Work out the probability that at least one of them is a toffee.

Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form.
hints: The only outcome with no toffee is mint then mint.
Take that away from 1.
parts.workedSolution: The one outcome with no toffee is mint then mint: $\tfrac{8}{13} \times \tfrac{7}{12} = \tfrac{56}{156}$, which is $\tfrac{14}{39}$. So $P(\text{at least one toffee}) = 1 - \tfrac{14}{39} = \tfrac{25}{39}$. Adding the other three branches gives $100/156$, the same fraction.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the probability of no toffee at all. Everything else has at least one, so subtract it from 1: $1 - \tfrac{14}{39} = \tfrac{25}{39}$.
That is exactly one toffee. At least one also allows two toffees, so that branch belongs in the total as well.

The tree diagram is for two counters taken at random, without replacement, from $7$ blue and $5$ yellow counters.

Does the number of yellows change?

parts.stem:
Niamh has a jar holding $6$ red beads and $5$ green beads.

She takes a bead at random and does not put it back. She then takes a second bead at random.

Work out the probability that her two beads are the same colour.

Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form.
hints: Same colour means both red or both green.
Work out each one, then add them.
The second denominator is one less than the first.
parts.workedSolution: Both red: $\tfrac{6}{11} \times \tfrac{5}{10} = \tfrac{30}{110}$. Both green: $\tfrac{5}{11} \times \tfrac{4}{10} = \tfrac{20}{110}$. Adding: $\tfrac{30}{110} + \tfrac{20}{110} = \tfrac{50}{110}$, which is $\tfrac{5}{11}$.

commonErrors.feedback: Both denominators stayed at $11$, so the bead was replaced. Each second-pick denominator is $10$, and the numerator falls too because the same colour was taken.
That is both red only. Both green is a second way of being the same colour, and it has to be added on.
The two branches were multiplied. Either branch will do, so they are added instead.

parts.stem:
A box holds $9$ batteries. $3$ of them are flat and the rest are good.

Two batteries are taken from the box at random, without replacement.

Complete the tree diagram.

rubric: First pair of branches labelled flat and good, with 3/9 and 6/9
Second branches after a flat: 2/8 and 6/8
Second branches after a good one: 3/8 and 5/8
Every branch carries both a label and a probability, and each pair sums to 1

hints: The first denominators are $9$.
Every second denominator is $8$.
Each pair of branches must add to 1.
parts.workedSolution: First pick: $P(\text{flat}) = \tfrac{3}{9}$, $P(\text{good}) = \tfrac{6}{9}$. After a flat battery: $\tfrac{2}{8}$ flat and $\tfrac{6}{8}$ good. After a good one: $\tfrac{3}{8}$ flat and $\tfrac{5}{8}$ good. Each pair adds to 1.

commonErrors.feedback: Every branch needs a label and a probability. A tree with the numbers missing cannot earn the marks that follow from it.

parts.stem:
Work out the probability that exactly one of the two batteries is flat.

Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form.

scheme.for: both orders used: 18/72 and 18/72, from their tree

hints: Exactly one flat can happen two ways.
Multiply along each branch, then add.
parts.workedSolution: Flat then good is $\tfrac{3}{9} \times \tfrac{6}{8} = \tfrac{18}{72}$, and good then flat is $\tfrac{6}{9} \times \tfrac{3}{8} = \tfrac{18}{72}$. Adding gives $\tfrac{36}{72} = \tfrac{1}{2}$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is flat first, working second. The other order counts too, so both products are added.
Along a branch both things happen, so the two probabilities multiply. Adding them gives a number far too large.

parts.stem:
Work out the probability that at least one of the two batteries is flat.

Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form.

scheme.for: 1 - 30/72, or the three matching branches added

hints: The only outcome with no flat battery is good then good.
Subtract that from 1.
parts.workedSolution: $P(\text{neither flat})$ is $\tfrac{6}{9} \times \tfrac{5}{8} = \tfrac{30}{72}$, which is $\tfrac{5}{12}$, so $P(\text{at least one flat}) = 1 - \tfrac{5}{12} = \tfrac{7}{12}$. The long route gives $6 + 18 + 18 = 42$ over $72$, the same fraction.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the probability that neither battery is flat. Subtract it from 1: $1 - \tfrac{5}{12} = \tfrac{7}{12}$.
That is exactly one flat battery, which is part (b). At least one also includes both being flat.

questions.solutionProgram: tree for 3 flat of 9; exactly one = 18/72 + 18/72 = 1/2; at least one = 1 - 30/72 = 7/12

parts.stem:
A tin holds $3$ plain biscuits, $4$ chocolate biscuits and $5$ ginger biscuits.

Two biscuits are taken from the tin at random.

Work out the probability that both biscuits are ginger.

Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form.
hints: Two taken at random: the second is out of one fewer.
Both ginger is one branch: multiply along it.

commonErrors.feedback: That keeps 12 under the second pick, as if the first biscuit went back. Two taken at random leaves 11, with 4 of them ginger.
Both biscuits have to be ginger, one after the other: multiply along the branch, do not add.
The bottom fell to 11, but the top must fall too: one ginger has gone, so 4 are left.

parts.stem: Work out the probability that the two biscuits are different types.

scheme.for: 38/132 seen as the same-type total, or 94/132

hints: Different types fits six branches; the same type fits three.
Work out the same type and take it from 1.
parts.workedSolution: Same type: $\tfrac{6}{132} + \tfrac{12}{132} + \tfrac{20}{132}$, which is $\tfrac{38}{132}$. Different types: $1 - \tfrac{38}{132} = \tfrac{94}{132}$, which is $\tfrac{47}{66}$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the probability of two of the same type. Different types is what is left when it is taken from 1.
Each mixed pair can come in either order, so each product counts twice. The quicker route is 1 minus the same type.
That keeps 12 under the second pick, as if the first biscuit went back.

context.setting: A bag of red, blue and one white counter

parts.stem:
A bag holds $2$ red counters, $2$ blue counters and $1$ white counter.

Two counters are taken at random.

Work out the probability that the two colours differ.

Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form.

scheme.for: $\frac{2}{5} \times \frac{1}{4}$ for each of red-red and blue-blue (white-white cannot happen)

hints: With one white counter, white then white cannot happen.
Find the same colour, then take it from 1.
parts.workedSolution: Same colour: red-red $\tfrac{2}{20}$ and blue-blue $\tfrac{2}{20}$; white-white is impossible. So the same colour is $\tfrac{4}{20}$ and different colours is $1 - \tfrac{4}{20} = \tfrac{16}{20} = \tfrac{4}{5}$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the same colour. Different colours is 1 minus it.
Each mixed pair can come in either order, so each counts twice.
Keeping 5 under the second pick puts the first counter back, and even lets white come twice.

figures.alt: A tree for whether Maeve's bus is late and whether she misses registration. The branch for a late bus carries 0.15; every other probability is an empty dotted box.

parts.stem:
The probability that Maeve's bus is late is $0.15$.

If the bus is late, the probability that she misses registration is $0.8$.

If the bus is not late, the probability that she misses registration is $0.05$.

Complete the tree diagram.

rubric: After not late: misses 0.05, in time 0.95
Each pair of branches adds to 1

scheme.for: 0.85 on the not-late branch and the pair after a late bus, 0.8 and 0.2
The pair after a bus that is not late, 0.05 and 0.95

hints: Each 'if' sentence belongs to its own first branch.
Each pair of branches from one point adds to 1.
parts.workedSolution: Not late: $1 - 0.15 = 0.85$. After a late bus: misses $0.8$, in time $0.2$. After a bus that is not late: misses $0.05$, in time $0.95$.

parts.stem: Work out the probability that Maeve misses registration.
hints: Missing registration happens two ways.
Multiply along each branch, then add.

commonErrors.feedback: That is only the late-bus branch. She can also miss registration when the bus is on time, so that branch is added.
Those are the two 'if' chances on their own. Each is multiplied by its first branch before they are added.
The not-late branch carries 0.85, not 0.15.

context.setting: Roses and lilies at a garden centre, some in flower

parts.stem:
A garden centre has $180$ plants: $100$ roses and $80$ lilies.

The probability that a rose is in flower is $0.3$. The probability that a lily is in flower is $\tfrac{3}{4}$.

A plant that is in flower is chosen at random.

Work out the probability that it is a lily.

Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form.
hints: Turn each probability into a number of plants first.
The plant is chosen from those in flower.
parts.workedSolution: Roses in flower: $0.3 \times 100 = 30$. Lilies in flower: $\tfrac{3}{4} \times 80 = 60$. In flower: $90$. So $P(\text{lily}) = \tfrac{60}{90} = \tfrac{2}{3}$.

commonErrors.feedback: That divides by every plant. The plant is chosen from those in flower, so those go on the bottom.
That is the chance that a lily is in flower, not the chance that a flowering plant is a lily.
That is the chance that a plant is in flower. The question then chooses from those plants: how many of them are lilies?

findTheMistake.stem: Sean was asked: a bag holds $8$ mints and $5$ toffees, and two sweets are taken without replacement. Work out the probability that both are mints. His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 1 is right. Line 2 uses the first-pick probability again, which is what happens when a sweet is put back. Without replacement the first mint stays out, so $8 - 1 = 7$ mints are left among $13 - 1 = 12$ sweets.
findTheMistake.feedback: Reading the words 'without replacement' and writing the second denominator down before anything else is what protects this mark. The method mark survives, because the structure of the working is right.

findTheMistake.stem: Aoife was asked: a box holds $4$ dark and $6$ milk chocolates, and two are taken without replacement. Work out the probability that both are dark. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 1 has both branch probabilities right and earns the method mark. Line 2 adds them. Along a branch both things have to happen, so the probabilities multiply; adding them here gives $11/15$, which is larger than $\tfrac{1}{2}$ even though taking two dark chocolates from a box that is mostly milk should be unlikely.
findTheMistake.feedback: A quick sense check catches this one: the answer should be well under a half, and it is not. Along a branch, multiply; across branches, add.

findTheMistake.stem: Niall was asked: a bag holds $3$ blue and $4$ white beads, and two are taken at random. Work out the probability that both beads match in colour. His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: He added the tops, 3 + 2 = 5, but multiplied the bottoms. When fractions are multiplied, the tops multiply too: 3 × 2 = 6, so blue then blue is 6/42.
findTheMistake.feedback: The reports on the non-calculator paper keep finding this slip, not the method: multiply top by top and bottom by bottom, and cancel first where you can. The white product and the adding still earn their marks.

prompts.prompt: Two items are taken without replacement. What happens to the numerator and the denominator on the second pick?
prompts.answer: The denominator always falls by one. The numerator falls by one only if the same type was taken first.

prompts.prompt: On a tree diagram, when do you multiply and when do you add?
prompts.answer: Multiply along a branch, because both events happen. Add across branches, because either one will do.

prompts.prompt: How do you work out the probability of at least one of something?
prompts.answer: Find the probability of none of it, and subtract that from 1.

prompts.prompt: A question asks for one of each colour. Why is one product not enough?
prompts.answer: Because either colour can come first. Both orders are separate branches and both have to be added.

prompts.prompt: A bag holds $7$ blue and $5$ yellow counters. Two are taken without replacement. What is $P(\text{both blue})$?
Your answer to a probability question comes out greater than 1. What has probably happened?
prompts.answer: Probabilities have been added along a branch instead of multiplied. Nothing that is a probability can exceed 1.

prompts.prompt: How should a probability be written on the answer line?
prompts.answer: As a fraction, a decimal or a percentage, and never as a ratio such as 3 : 8.

prompts.prompt: Why is it worth cancelling before multiplying two fractions on the non-calculator paper?
prompts.answer: Because the numbers stay small, and the reports name fraction multiplication as the usual place marks are lost.

prompts.prompt: Without replacement, what happens to the second pick's numerator and denominator?
prompts.answer: Denominator falls by one; numerator falls only if the same type was taken.

prompts.prompt: How do you find the probability of at least one?
prompts.answer: Work out the probability of none, and take it from 1.

prompts.prompt: A question asks for one of each colour. Why is one product not enough?
prompts.answer: Either colour can come first, so both orders count: add both products.

prompts.prompt: A probability answer comes out greater than 1. What has probably happened?
prompts.answer: Probabilities were added along a branch instead of multiplied; none can exceed 1.

prompts.prompt: How should a probability be written on the answer line?
prompts.answer: As a fraction, a decimal or a percentage, never as a ratio.

prompts.prompt: Why cancel before multiplying fractions on the non-calculator paper?
prompts.answer: The numbers stay small; the reports say marks go in fraction multiplication.

findings.asked: Non-replacement probabilities: show a given result, then a further probability.
findings.wentWrong: Most knew which products to form and over half added them correctly; fraction multiplication was the weakness.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Cancelled before multiplying and reached the further probability by subtracting the opposite event from 1.
findings.rule: Practise multiplying fractions by hand: the method marks depend on it.

findings.asked: Multiply three probabilities for a repeated event.
findings.wentWrong: Many added instead of multiplying, or could not multiply three simple fractions; some did two repetitions instead of three.

findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Wrote the second-pick fractions down before multiplying anything.
findings.rule: Denominator drops by one each pick; numerator drops if the same type was taken.

findings.wentWrong: A third got it; a third forgot the outcomes could occur in either order; a third had no idea what to do with the probabilities.
findings.rule: Both orders unless the question fixes the order.

findings.asked: A high-grade probability where pairs of numbers can be chosen in either order.
findings.wentWrong: Only the best recognised the suitable pairs and doubled for order.
findings.rule: Count the pairs, then count the orders.

findings.asked: A probability problem without a calculator.
findings.wentWrong: Majority full marks; losses came from poor fraction multiplication.
findings.rule: Cancel before multiplying to keep the numbers small.

findings.wentWrong: Over 70 per cent full marks, which the report puts down to good teaching.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Drew the tree, multiplied along each branch and added the branches that fitted.
findings.rule: Tree, multiply along, add the matching branches.

findings.asked: A wordy probability: group sizes and a probability for each, then a choice from those who fit.
findings.wentWrong: About half worked it through; most of the rest started but could not carry the information to a conclusion.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Turned each probability into a number of people first, then divided by the group the choice was made from.
findings.rule: Count first, then choose from the right group.

findings.asked: Draw a tree for a biased dice rolled twice, then read a probability from it.
findings.wentWrong: Over 80 per cent drew a correct tree; the common error was leaving the labels off.
findings.rule: Every branch carries a label and a probability.

insight.ruleToRemember: Without replacement, denominators fall by one at each pick and numerators fall only when the same type was taken; multiply along each branch, add the branches that fit, include every order, and cancel before multiplying.
insight.aStarSignal: Non-calculator fraction products for three picks without replacement, with the orders counted and 'at least one' answered by subtracting the opposite event from 1.
